title: Software factories are only the beginning: AI's real payoff is Renaissance-style meticulous refinement
dek: Thariq Shihipar says AI is both an industrial revolution that makes software cheap and a Renaissance that makes it worthwhile to polish every detail—and both should happen simultaneously in the same project.
why: No fresh data, but a concrete, usable methodology: a scripting language for the /human folder that reintegrates human feedback loops back into vibe coding—practical for anyone leading teams building products with agents.
who: Independent developers and product people building personal projects or products with agents who want methods for refining product feel, and practitioners interested in RSI and decision model applications.
skip: 20:32-27:50 — technical debate about decision models and large language model intelligence is granular; skip if you're not chasing cutting-edge reasoning details.

points.h: Vibe coding surrenders your ability to control what your software does
points.body: While building a game, Thariq discovered that models generate behaviors based on reasonable assumptions, yet he often couldn't predict what a character would do in a given situation—the loss of control made him uncomfortable. His solution: create a /human folder with a specialized scripting language emphasizing high-density comments, banning single-letter variables, and limiting line length. The goal is code that reads like a spec but runs directly—he can tweak it and rebuild his understanding of what the system actually does.

points.h: AI is industrial revolution and Renaissance—they must coexist in one project
points.body: Thariq frames 2026 as the "software factory" year: AI brings efficiency, reliability, and scale, but also slop. The next phase is the "Renaissance": redirecting savings toward marginal quality—refining control schemes, building niche customizations, adding personal style to work. These aren't alternatives; they coexist in the same project: the bottom layer runs industrial optimization, the surface layer gets meticulous craftsmanship.

points.h: Perfect balance makes games boring—variance, not equilibrium, creates fun
points.body: Testing his card game Frontier Lab through thousands of simulations, Thariq found the economic victory path always dominates. When he asked the model to fix this imbalance, it performed poorly. His conclusion: good game design doesn't eliminate all imbalance, it introduces variance—like roguelikes that let usually-weak strategies win in certain runs. That variance, not mathematical perfection, makes games engaging.

points.h: The bottleneck is not tokens or intelligence, but how we work with models
points.body: Thariq is unambiguous: he's not constrained by token counts or intelligence ceilings—he even wonders if the real limit is not thinking big enough. The genuine bottleneck is the working model itself: how to collaborate with models. This is why he built the /human scripting language—not because models lack power, but because existing human-AI interfaces are still primitive.

points.h: Decision models occupy the middle ground between hard-coded rules and full reasoning loops
points.body: He maps AI behavior design as a spectrum: fully hard-coded rules on one end, tool-calling loops doing reasoning at every step on the other. Decision models sit in the middle—you pre-write most of the behavior tree, then use one forward pass to decide which branch the current state should follow, only escalating to full reasoning when necessary. For scenarios like customer service that are fundamentally decision trees, decision-model-first architectures should be the priority now.

points.h: Adoption is unprecedented, but nothing macroscopic has fundamentally changed
points.body: Thariq acknowledges agent adoption is the fastest on record, and public data show Anthropic transformed this year. Yet he emphasizes there's been no 10% GDP growth, no major labor market shock—software remains hard to build. He compares it to the smartphone revolution 15 years ago: in one sense the world completely changed, in another sense nothing changed at all. It's not a slow takeoff—it's acceleration without the feeling of liftoff.

points.h: RSI's best future turns scientific research into knowledge work
points.body: On recursive self-improvement, Thariq questions whether fully autonomous execution is even optimal. His vision for better division of labor: AI handles hard technical work—efficiency, safety—and automates fields still mired in dirty-wet-lab chaos like biology. Humans pivot toward "knowledge work": making decisions, allocating resources, securing support. Like how running a restaurant became white-collar work, this is the future he sees as better for humanity.

points.h: Young people need new achievement prosthetics as traditional status ladders disappear
points.body: Citing Simon Saris: video games are a "prosthetic for achievement" for youth—no one trusts an ambitious teenager with genuine high-stakes work, but they can lead a World of Warcraft guild and practice organizing people, setting deadlines, solving puzzles. Thariq has noticed many people in RL and pretraining were former WoW guild leaders. He raises an open question: as school grades and GitHub commit histories stop being clear status ladders, what will young people use to prove they can handle real responsibility?

terms.def: A small model that makes judgments with a single forward pass rather than chain-of-thought reasoning, commonly used for routing and fast decisions.
The cycle where AI models participate in improving the development process of next-generation models themselves.
Games and activities that substitute for genuine high-stakes responsibility, allowing young people to practice organization and decision-making skills early.
